content: Pubic hair refers to the hair that grows in the frontal genital region, the crotch, and sometimes the upper inner thighs, collectively known as the pubic region. While fine vellus hair is present in this area during childhood, the term pubic hair specifically refers to the coarser, longer hair that develops during puberty due to increased androgen levels. This type of hair is classified as androgenic hair. Development of Pubic Hair Before puberty, both boys and girls have fine, soft vellus hair in the genital area, which is categorized as Tanner stage 1 hair. As puberty begins, the body produces higher levels of androgens, which stimulate the skin in the genital region to grow thicker, often curlier hair with a faster growth rate. The initial appearance of pubic hair is referred to as pubarche. Although the transformation of individual hair follicles is relatively rapid, the overall area of skin covered by androgenic hair expands gradually over several years. In females, pubic hair typically first appears along the edges of the labia majora (Tanner stage 2) and then spreads forward to cover the mons pubis (Tanner stage 3) over the next two years. By the time most girls reach menarche (approximately 2-3 years into puberty), the pubic triangle is densely covered with hair. Within another two years, pubic hair often extends to the upper inner thighs and, in some cases, forms a thin line of hair extending upward toward the umbilicus. In males, the initial appearance of pubic hair is observed as a few sparse hairs on the scrotum or at the upper base of the penis (Tanner stage 2). Within a year, the hair around the base of the penis becomes denser and more numerous (Tanner stage 3). Over the next 3-4 years, the pubic area becomes fully covered with thicker, darker hair (Tanner stage 4), and by approximately five years into puberty, the hair extends to the upper inner thighs and upward toward the umbilicus (Tanner stage 5). Other areas of the body also respond to androgens, though with slightly less sensitivity, leading to the development of androgenic hair in a sequential pattern. This typically begins with the armpits (axillae), followed by the perianal region, upper lip, sideburns (preauricular areas), areas around the nipples (periareolar regions), the middle of the chest, the neck under the chin, the remainder of the chest and beard area, the limbs and shoulders, the back, and the buttocks. Although pubarche is often considered part of puberty, it is a distinct process that is independent of gonadal maturation, which leads to sexual maturity and fertility. Pubic hair can develop solely in response to adrenal androgens, even in cases where the ovaries or testes are nonfunctional. For more details, refer to the broader topic of puberty. Variations in Pubic Hair The ability of male and female bodies to grow hair in response to androgens is largely similar. However, the noticeable differences in hair distribution between men and women are primarily due to variations in androgen levels during and after puberty. Patterns of pubic hair growth can vary significantly among individuals. Some people have thick, coarse pubic hair, while others have sparse, fine hair. The texture of pubic hair ranges from tightly curled to completely straight. These patterns can also differ based on race and ethnicity. The color of pubic hair often differs from scalp hair. In most individuals, pubic hair is darker, though it can also be lighter. In women, the pubic hair typically forms a triangular patch over the mons pubis, also known as the mons veneris or mound of Venus. In men, the pubic hair often tapers upward into a line of hair pointing toward the navel, forming a more upward-pointing triangular shape. Similar to axillary (armpit) hair, pubic hair is associated with a high concentration of sebaceous glands in the region.
